div.div:
1.The browser creates a subscription (with the push service's infrastructure) by sending it our server's public key,
The push services send the globally unique subscribtion token back to the browser, after storing in their database
Then this subscribtion token need to be stored by our server to send the push event to that browser later on
The server public key is used by the push services for verifing the jwt sent by our server signed with private key, thus proving the server identify

div.div:
The endpoint is unique per (browser instance + origin + service worker subscription) — not per user. That means:
Every time a different browser/profile calls .subscribe(), Google's FCM backend mints a brand-new unique registration ID and endpoint — even though they're all using the identical applicationServerKey.

div.div:
The subscription stays valid indefinitely as long as:
The user doesn't uninstall/clear the PWA or clear site data
The service worker registration isn't unregistered
Chrome doesn't internally rotate the underlying FCM token (which it can do periodically, silently, for its own key-management reasons — usually every few months, but there's no published fixed interval)

p.font: Yes — that endpoint URL is itself a pointer into Google's infrastructure, not just an opaque string.

strong.font: How it works on Google's side:

li.font: fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send/<registration-id> — that <registration-id> (the long token after /send/) is a key into Google's FCM backend database, mapping it to: the specific browser instance, the origin (your localhost:5173 / eventually printcampus.in), the associated public key (p256dh), and delivery routing info.

div.div: Before VAPID, browser push services had no way to know who was sending a push message or to rate-limit/contact a sender if something went wrong. VAPID fixes this by having your server sign each push request with a private key, so the push service can verify it came from you.

div.p: You generate one ECDSA key pair (P-256 curve) for your entire application:

ul.class: [li_&]:mb-0 [li_&]:mt-1 [li_&]:gap-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ul]:pb-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ol]:pb-1 list-disc flex flex-col gap-1 pl-8 mb-3 print:block print:space-y-1
ul.li: Public key: sent to the browser when you call pushManager.subscribe(). It gets baked into the subscription — the push service (e.g. Google's FCM endpoint) associates this public key with that specific subscription.
Private key: stays on your server, never exposed. You use it to sign a JWT for every push message you send.

div.p: navigator.serviceWorker is a ServiceWorkerContainer — one per page, tied to the page's own URL/scope. .ready is a promise that resolves once there is an active service worker controlling this page. It doesn't take an argument telling it which SW to wait for — it just looks at whatever registration applies to the current page's scope.

Since sw1.js was the only thing registered for this page, and its scope covers this page, .ready resolves to that same registration — same object, in effect, as what register("./sw/sw1.js") created. That's the connection: implicit, via scope-matching done internally by the browser, not via a shared JS variable.

div.p: Push is fundamentally different from something like a WebSocket where the connection is the identity — here, the browser generates this subscription once at subscribe-time and then goes silent. Your server has no live connection to the client at all. The only way to reach a specific rider later (say, when their order status changes) is to already have their subscription object sitting in your DB, looked up by riderId.

p.strong: Two things worth planning for since you're storing these long-term

ol.class: [li_&]:mb-0 [li_&]:mt-1 [li_&]:gap-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ul]:pb-1 [&:not(:last-child)_ol]:pb-1 list-decimal flex flex-col gap-1 pl-8 mb-3 print:block print:space-y-1
ol.li: One rider, multiple subscriptions. If a rider opens your rider-web-app on both their phone and a desktop browser, each is a separate subscription (different endpoint/keys). Store as one-to-many, not one-to-one, or you'll silently overwrite one device's subscription with another's.

Subscriptions expire/die silently. Push services return 410 Gone (or sometimes 404) when a subscription is no longer valid (user cleared site data, uninstalled, browser revoked it, etc.). You won't know until you try to send — so on that response code, delete the row from your DB rather than retrying it forever.
